nameStory: This plant gets its name from its leaves, which look remarkably similar to those of hyssop, an aromatic herb used in cooking and medicine. The 'hedge-nettle' part comes from its preference for growing along hedgerows and edges, though despite the name, it doesn't actually sting like true nettles do. It's a case of mistaken identity that stuck!
description: Hyssop-leaved hedge-nettle is a modest member of the mint family that stands about 1-3 feet tall. It has the characteristic square stems that give away its mint family heritage, topped with spikes of small tubular flowers. The narrow, lance-shaped leaves grow in opposite pairs up the stem, giving the whole plant a neat, organized appearance. Unlike some of its showier mint relatives, this one tends to blend quietly into the background of New England's wild spaces.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel the stem between your fingers - it's distinctly square with four flat sides, a telltale sign of the mint family. The stems feel smooth to slightly rough and are often tinged with purple or red.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves grow in opposite pairs, each leaf about 2-4 inches long with small teeth along the edges. They feel somewhat rough and have visible veins running parallel to the leaf edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers cluster in interrupted whorls around the upper stem, creating a spike-like appearance. The flowers are typically white to pale pink with purple spots, and each has the characteristic two-lipped shape of mint flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small colonies through underground runners, creating patches of upright stems. The plant has a neat, unbranched appearance with all the action happening at the top where the flowers bloom.

habitat: Look for hyssop-leaved hedge-nettle in wetland edges, stream banks, and moist meadows throughout New England. It particularly enjoys the transition zones between wet and dry areas, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll find it in both sunny and partially shaded spots, as long as the soil stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge as the weather warms, showing off those distinctive square stems early. The opposite leaves unfurl in neat pairs, making identification possible even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time brings the small white to pale pink flowers arranged in their characteristic interrupted spikes. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small nutlet seeds develop, while the leaves may begin to yellow. The square stems remain obvious even as the plant starts to wind down for winter.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving no trace until spring's return. Only the underground runners persist through New England's cold months.

funFact: Despite being called a 'hedge-nettle,' this plant is completely harmless to touch and actually belongs to the same family as basil, oregano, and mint - you might even detect a faint minty smell if you crush the leaves!
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with other hedge-nettles in the Stachys genus, but hyssop-leaved hedge-nettle has narrower leaves than marsh hedge-nettle and lacks the woolly fuzz of woolly hedge-nettle. Remember: narrow leaves like hyssop, square stems like mint, and always in moist spots.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'hedge-nettle' is misleading since these plants don't sting at all - they're named for their preference for growing along hedgerows and their somewhat nettle-like leaf shape. This naming confusion has led many people to avoid a perfectly harmless plant that's actually quite pleasant to encounter in the wild.
compareHints: Among its hedge-nettle relatives, this species stands out for its narrow, hyssop-like leaves and preference for wetter habitats. Marsh hedge-nettle has broader, more heart-shaped leaves, while woolly hedge-nettle is covered in soft, silvery hairs. If you see narrow leaves and wet feet, you've likely found the hyssop-leaved species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Marsh woundwort differs from its hedge-nettle cousins by its preference for consistently wet habitats rather than just moist woodland edges.
Unlike other hedgenettles in New England, woolly hedgenettle is the only one with thick, densely woolly leaves that feel soft to touch.
Among New England's hedge nettles, marsh hedge nettle stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, soft-textured leaves and stems compared to its smoother relatives.
Prairie woundwort differs from marsh woundwort by preferring dry rather than wet habitats and having broader, more heart-shaped leaves.
